extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, law students, and legal scholars addressing damages/accounting for patent infringement
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary rules for computing and apportioning profits/damages in actions for patent infringement, covering sales of articles embodying inventions, increased sales due to an invention, and profits from use/manufacture. Addresses burdens of proof, apportionment, and limits on recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profit measure for patented feature embodied in a sold article
rubrics_metrics.description: The price paid for the patented invention is the price received for the whole article less what it would have brought in open market had the patented invention been omitted. Its cost is the difference between the expense of making the article with it and without it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute profit by subtracting excess cost from excess price. If price remains the same but expense of manufacture is lessened, profit is the decrease in cost. If cost and price are unchanged (or change proportionally), there is no profit on a single article attributable to the patented invention; any benefit must arise from increased sales. Examples and case citations illustrate application (e.g., where the patented feature is a separable component vs. part of a larger machine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits attributable when invention increases number or amount of sales (§1141)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the presence of the patented invention, though adding nothing to the profit on a single article, increases the number of the defendant's sales, all the profits on those articles which would not have been sold but for the invention are due to the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such articles can be separated, compute their profits as price received minus cost of manufacture. If separation is impossible, profits cannot be computed or recovered. Where the invention opens new uses/market lines, the marketable group attributable to the invention may be distinguishable and profits ascertainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire market value rule — whole profit when invention gives entire marketability (§1142)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the article, though containing other features, so far derives its marketability from the invention that articles without it would be unsalable, the entire profit on the sales must be attributed to the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Market value (price commanded in open market) differs from mere salability. When the patented feature gives an article its entire market value, courts may award entire profits; cited cases and judicial hesitations are noted. Illustrations include cases where a slight patented improvement makes an otherwise unsalable large article sellable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment where part of selling price derives from other matter
rubrics_metrics.description: When a portion of the selling price is due to other matter than the plaintiff's invention, the cost (and profit) attributable to that other matter must be deducted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On combination patents, recover only the profits caused by the exact new features covered by the patent. The plaintiff must separate the patented feature's contribution from other portions of the article; evidence must be tangible, not speculative, to apportion profits properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery limited to profits on exact new features (combination patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: On a patent for a combination only the profits on the exact new features of the invention can be recovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patented improvement is only one constituent part of a machine, profits are confined to what can be shown to be made by the manufacture and sale of the patented part separately (or otherwise attributable specifically to it). Cases show courts will not arbitrarily divide monopoly profits among parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits from unpatented elements sometimes recoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits due to an element not patented, which enters into the composition of patented articles, are sometimes allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although recovery generally focuses on patented features, courts have recognized situations where unpatented elements that form part of the infringing article's composition may justify inclusion of some profits; case law governs when this is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof — plaintiff must prove defendant's profits and their amount (§1143)
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof concerning the receipt of profits by the defendant from sale of the patented invention, and their precise amount, devolves upon the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must show by a preponderance of testimony the exact sum for which the defendant is accountable. Defendant may be examined, books inspected, and other investigative methods pursued, but the affirmative proof of receipts and expenditures rests on the plaintiff. If plaintiff fails, only nominal damages may be awarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits must be ascertained by computation from definite data
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits are ascertained by computation, and computation requires certain data (price received and cost of producing it) to which arithmetical processes may be applied with definite and invariable results; they are not a matter of speculation or arbitrary adjustment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require concrete data (receipts and expenditures) enabling subtraction to determine profit. Arbitrary awards (e.g., simply assigning half the net profits) are improper. Evidence must enable a mathematical determination rather than conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of evidence required — direct or conclusive circumstantial; no conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence upon these points must be direct; or, if circumstantial, the inferences drawn therefrom must be conclusive. The evidence must show the amount of profits and not leave them open to conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff should provide tangible, reliable proofs separating patented-feature profits from others. Courts will inspect books and examine witnesses, but in absence of adequate proof, an accounting of profits cannot be ordered. Design-patent cases require especially clear separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: If profits cannot be determined, only nominal damages
rubrics_metrics.description: When the profits cannot be determined by evidence they cannot be recovered as damages; only nominal damages and injunction relief remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difficulty or expense of proof does not excuse lack of measurement. Cases hold that profits must be capable of measurement; where they are not, recovery for profits is denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalties are not a reliable measure of profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Royalties paid by the defendant or others do not afford a measure of profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payments of royalties do not substitute for the concrete computation of receipts and expenses required to show profits attributable to infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of profits where infringement consists of use or manufacture-and-use (§1144)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the infringing act consists in unlawful use or making and use of the patented invention, the benefit rarely assumes the form of a specific sum and may appear as increased receipts or decreased expenses; different rules apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Profits from use may take form of direct gains or savings; cost of using may be ascertainable but value of the use often requires more complicated rules (e.g., estimating increase in price commanded or cost savings achieved).

rubrics_metrics.name: Receipts and savings can be used as the minuend only in limited cases (§1145)
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire amount received or saved by the defendant cannot be taken as the minuend except in peculiar cases: if defendant is paid a definite sum for using the invention, if product can be produced only by the infringing process/machine, or if the saving cannot be accomplished by any other method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Otherwise the advantage is measured only by the additional value conferred by the patented idea over methods already available to the public; if other means could have secured similar receipts/savings, deduct what would have been obtained by those prior means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of use limited to the addition beyond prior public means
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of the use of an invention is the value of the new idea or means which the inventor has embodied — i.e., the addition to human knowledge and convenience to which only the patent extends; benefits obtainable by means open to the public at the invention date are not attributable to the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute profits by taking defendant's receipts/savings and deducting whatever would have been received/saved by using prior public means. The doctrine ignores prior or subsequent patents/licenses that an infringer might have used or obtained—plaintiff's patent secures exclusive use of his invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant cannot escape liability by pointing to other available inventions/licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of other prior patented inventions that the defendant had or could have acquired rights to does not affect the apportionment; the plaintiff's patent secures exclusive use and defendants who use it without right remain accountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will not permit the defendant to palliate infringement by arguing that they could have obtained other patents or subsequent inventions; the inquiry focuses on the advantage the infringer obtained from use of the plaintiff's invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-patent special considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule of separating profits due to patented feature is even more applicable to a patent for design than for mechanism; ornamentation or pattern may affect marketability, but the patentee must show how much profit is attributable to the design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design patents require the patentee to separate and apportion benefits of the design from other merits; courts are cautious about attributing entire profits to a pattern absent factual proof that profit should be so attributed.
